p: A little bit of a bump. And for the retention piece, does MOPD then provide support to those who may not be able to continue working or are having challenges?

Yeah. So, the staff has a year for retention services. If people want to find a new job, etcetera, and I think that’s fantastic, because retention is important and having that timeline is really helpful.
And have retention services been used?
Yes, used all the time by employees.
Got it. And the budget for this projected fiscal cycle, is that enough?

It– yeah. I think that if we want to expand then we may want– the way this began, At Work, was for private funding, and then it was so successful that we got City Tax Levy. And so if we need to, we can go to private funders and explore expanding that money.
And then is there funding specifically within that bucket for community outreach and engagement? I’d love to know just the demographic breakdown of who you all are serving.
Yeah. We can get more in those– that information, but the work that the six people do is immense, and they do trainings, outreach, so many stuff, and so I’ll share the details afterwards.
Got it. And has there been specific outreach plans made to ensure that the pool of New Yorkers is diverse.
I think so.
Can you share a little bit more?

So, on an annual basis we anonymize the data of job-seekers with disabilities and sort of analyze the demographic of the job-seekers that have been connected through NYC At Work. So, after this hearing, we’re happy to share that data with you.

Yeah. I wish you were prepared to share that right now, because it is I think very important to understand who within the disability community is being served and not being served and why they’re not and how we can reach them and make sure that they’re not left out. So, we will

wait for those details. Coming to education now. Local Law 18 passed in 2023 mandated that the city create an electronic system for New York City Public Schools to share documentation to help special needs students secure their necessary accommodations when they move on to higher education. New York City public schools created this system in collaboration with MOPD. Could you describe MOPD’s role in developing this system?

Yeah, so the New York Public Schools already had the technical infrastructure in place to implement the electronic systems required of the law, and because of that, Mayor’s Office of People with Disabilities deferred to public schools on the design, build-out, and day-to-day implementation of the platform. Our role was focused on providing guidance to ensure that the systems align with people with disabilities, principals, and comply with all of our relevant federal, state, city requirements.
So, the funding associated in developing this system was all New York City Public Schools?

Yes. But our end, we also provided a dedicated digital resource page on our website titled resource for students with disabilities transitioning to high school or higher education, and this page provided students and families with clear information about their resources, the documents that they may need and how to navigate the accommodations process when they move on to post secondary education.

And so for supporting education work and students across elementary, middle, high school, colleges, does MOPD have any additional funding for that work, or are you all relying on CUNY, public schools?

Yeah. I mean, I think again, we work with other agencies or CUNY to impact that coordinating with each other helps a lot. So, the public schools had the logistical avenues. We had the resources and training. So, working with agencies moves the ball more forward than with us just doing it alone.
Got it. But specifically on education, there isn’t any separate allocation to support that work.
No.

Got it. And that’s why you all don’t get credit. You all don’t get credit. It seems to me like you all should play even a much more influential role in partnerships with the public schools and CUNY, and not just the giving some feedback and be hidden in the background. And so I’d be really interested to know how you take on this work moving forward. And then what other collaborations are taking place with the DOE?
Yeah. So–
[interposing] And

And SCA. So, CUNY we do internship opportunities for CUNY students, promote hiring opportunities for CUNY and their alums. For DOE we work with D75 transition services to explore collaboration to get from transition students connected to opportunities through At Work, New York City At Work, and those are some of the ways that we are working with other agencies.
And then for the School Construction Authority, is there anything specific that you all are guiding them through when capital projects around accessibility—
Yeah, I don’t–

Well, it’s through the five-year accessibility plans. The physical– what we have every agency fill out their commitment to making sure that all their agency programs and services are accessible. So, one work stream is through the Five-Year Accessibility Plan, but also on a case-by-case basis. If we get any information about schools that are not accessible, then we work with the relevant agencies to, like, remediate those issues, including
But the work has to start with SCA before it comes to
Correct.
Yes.

Because so many of our schools are inaccessible, and getting them to become accessible has been a huge challenge for many of the locations. I know that my colleagues and I

have been funding accessible playgrounds and play yards, and they’re very, very costly. And similarly with adding ramps to schools and an elevator. Elevator costs millions of dollars, and it is really– it puts us behind. I think New York City must lead in disability justice, and if our schools are inaccessible and MOPD doesn’t play the influential role of really pushing for that policy, I think that’s a– it’s a disservice. I would like to see MOPD play a much more energetic role in pushing for accessible schools.

Yeah. And I agree, and also, information concerning accessible schools buildings is contained in a division-wide built accessible profile, or BAP, list on the DOE website. And so I would encourage you to read that out, but one of my goals is to meet with the chancellor and explore ideas that we can do together to expand children.

Wonderful. You all work with HPD as well to ensure that folks with disabilities are able to use Housing Connect and the housing lottery. The report from 2025 Accessible NYC

states that MOPD worked with HPD to ensure that the Housing Connect 2.0 platform is compatible for screen reader users. Could you talk about MOPD’s Housing COnnect compatibility efforts and is their funding associated with that work, or are you relying again on HPD’s funding to move this forward?

Yeah. So, our wonderful MOPD Digital Accessibility Coordinator worked with HPD to identify digital accessibility issues and provided recommendation solutions to HPD from the launch of the Housing Connect 2.0 until about fall of 2023. And the labor costs for this, MOPD, is just one individual who worked on that. And with– so I’ll just end there.
Got it. So, one staff person from MOPD has this in their portfolio, but I’m assuming that this person also has other relationships with agencies in their portfolios?
Yes.
And that staff person’s salary, does that take into account the work that’s happening with HPD or how is that determined?

I guess MOPD works with all agencies, and we– our role is coordinating agencies to do this work, accessibility and inclusion. And so that’s– our core area is coordinating, providing our expertise which is on accessibility and inclusion. We don’t want the– all of the agencies to do that work. We want agencies to do that work, and I have found that this with administration people are really excited to work with us and figure out a way to move it forward.
For the Housing Connect 2.0, what’s the budget dedicated to that effort?
I’m not sure about the exact budget. Do you know? We can find out.
But none of that funding would be coming from MOPD?
Yeah.
I just want to make it– make very clear–
[interposing] Yeah.
I understand the role that MOPD has. And then what additional housing support does MOPD provide?

Yeah. So, when constituents contact MOPD regarding housing-related matters, we refer to community-based organizations, DSS, PEU, HPD, DOB, all of the city services and nonprofits that are relevant for that individual. We have housing resources on our website, including resources– we have worked with other agencies on developing that. And some of these pamphlets, etcetera, I plan to review and update them as-needed.
And are you all keeping data on the folks who keep– who get in touch with you all around housing issues to make sure that they remain housed, or are able to find permanent housing?
We do, but if it’s somebody with supportive housing, we connect them to Health Department, but many times they call MOPD first, and then we direct where to go if they are needed.
Got it. So, in this instance, as well, MOPD is providing guidance on– or giving a referral, giving them a referral to reach out to HPD or the–
[interposing] Yes.

agency that would be tasked with completing their specific issue. And so I think– I’m just trying to understand, like, you know, you all have a very tiny budget, and you’re doing a lot of connecting. You’re doing a lot of connecting and it seems like the other agencies are following ADA guidelines. However, it’s not as though you all are the ones kind of identifying the problem or saying all of our schools should have elevators, or like a sort of accessibility policies or advocacy. Am I right to say that?

I would– so, in my vision, we do a lot of programs, but also impact. So, using laws, using relationships and using communications to message our thoughts out, that we do a little, but we want to do a lot more, and that’s the goal of my vision is having MOPD– MOPD’s ideas and vision available to agencies, but also to the

broader public so that they can refer to us, but I do not want our office to be another agency.
Yeah.

Because that means all that will be put into disabilities, and I think that we should have– we should work with agencies to ensure that they take their job. They don’t do like bare minimum, they do it the best of the class and style.

Understood. What steps has MOPD taken to ensure city agency websites and mobile applications are compliant with ADA digital disability standards ahead of the April 2026 federal rule-making, and does MOPD have a plan to enforce compliance across agencies that are currently out of compliance?
We are– we do the compliance and the Five-year Accessibility Plan, but I’ll find out anything more after this call– after this meeting.
And are you able to provide an assessment of which city agencies websites are currently compliant?
We can– I think we will tell you after this meeting.
Got it. And so that is something that you all are keeping track of.
Yes. Yes.
And then what is the timeline for the agencies that are not compliant, bringing them to compliance?

I can answer that. So, one of our staff resources is responsible for liaising with a lot of the IT departments of various agencies and making sure their agency’s websites and digital portals that are used to interact with the public are made accessible to the WCAG standards. And every two years, MOPD has a responsibility to publish the work that we do in that regard.
So, in that report–

[interposing] In that report, we don’s list out the agencies, but we list out the work that has been remediated, and it’s a little technical, but we can get you the list of agencies we work with, and we’re remediating a lot

of the digital assets that agencies have that interact with the public.
Got it. And for agencies that are not compliant, what are the obstacles?

Sometimes it’s technical, sometimes it’s financial. So, to reference Commissioner Agarawal when she mentioned that if we don’t get started on an agency’s project from the get-go as, like, advisors, then a lot of the agencies may roll out with a tool that after it’s put out to the public, the community comes and evaluates and provides feedback. And we take that feedback mechanism in– take that and then work with our partners to remediate those issues.
Got it. And you mentioned financial.

A lot of times when either a good or a service is procured that’s interacting with the public and it’s not accessible, it’s costly to retrofit them to make them accessible later. So, that’s the financial burdens that come into play once we get involved.
Got it. Are financial burdens going to prevent any of the agencies to not be in compliance?
It’s hard to say. It would depend on the agency or product or tool that we’re talking about.
Does each agency have their own funds towards accessible communications?
Not to our knowledge.
Would you know for the website, specifically, or the apps that they use, if there are separate budgets for that?

I’m not– I don’t know. We don’t know, but we’ll find out. I think it’s important also that this administration and the agencies that lead are– want to work with the Mayor’s Office of People with Disabilities. And so maybe in three months we’ll see some changes that will impact people with disabilities and the broader public. Because the reality is elevators impact me in a positive way, but impact people with kids, impact

older adults. It helps everyone and that’s the goal that we want to see for New York City.

Absolutely. And I would love to know which vendor is being used for the website, if there is one. Because all the– I’m assuming all the city agencies websites are one contractor, or are they different?
They’re probably different.

Okay. So, yeah, I think– you know, it would be interesting for me to just better understand given you all are providing this sort of oversight and compliance, that all of these agencies have a responsibility to ensure accessible website, and that they’re following the guidelines. And if there is a financial burden, what is that financial burden? And how can we remediate that so that we’re not– we’re not saying that funds are the reason why we can’t make something accessible for a city agency. You mentioned elevators. I want to talk about Access-A-Ride. What is your relationship with MTA?

Well, we are in constant consultation with MTA to improve Access-a-Ride, including on services reliant to people with disabilities. So, we advocate for the expansion fo Access-A-Ride on demand pilot. So, riders have more flexibility and independence. We provide– we direct rider feedback to the MTA through advisory meetings and general escalation. And we advise on accessibility improvements to Access-A-Ride vehicles and the digital tool called AAR App.

Got it. So that's a pretty good chunk of work that you all are doing with MTA. Are you hearing from New Yorkers or organizations that you all work with about obstacles they’re experiencing with MTA and Access-A-Ride?

Yeah. Some problems are– issues are unreliable, access-A-Ride pick-ups, and long unpredictable travel routes, limited subway accessibility, including elevators, etcetera, and gaps in accessible pedestrian infrastructure including the lack of curb cuts and insufficient crossing times. So, all that is like broader than Access-A-Ride, but that impacts people.
Is there other transportation-related work that MOPD is involved in?

Yeah. So, we work with DOT and we provide– we partner with DOT on monitoring issues related to accessible pedestrian signals, curb cuts, and accessible street design. We also work with TLC on expanding wheelchair accessible taxi services. And we work in interagency groups on transportation equity and pedestrian safety, and we review accessible in the mobile technology and pilot infrastructure.
And all that work also does not have a specific budget allocation?
Yes.
Got it. What additional transportation support do you hear about that New Yorkers need which MOPD could provide with some for funding?

Well, you know, again, for MOPD itself, I’ll talk to you, OMB, and City Hall, but we would like to collaborate with MTA on driver trainings for the para transit system to ensure drivers with mobility, sensory or cognitive

disabilities are better served. We also expand outreach and driver education, including disability-specific navigation tools, and we support for research and pilots and accessible new mobile technologies. So, those are some of the things we do.

That’s very helpful. Yeah, and that seems like it’s all really what we need to be up to date with these requirements. Could you share how many city employees are employed under 55A and under how many agencies?
As Commissioner Agarawal mentioned previously, there’s about 700 slots dedicated to the 55A program, and about half of them are filled currently.
And then what are you all doing to help the city reach the 700 goal?
Yeah. So, I’m meeting with the Commissioner of DCAS, and she and I both want to work on the impact with disabilities and having more people do 55A programs than half. We want to increase that.
And is there a timeline for–
[interposing] I’m meeting with her two weeks from now, so I’ll let you know.
Got it. Okay. I’m going to do one last review of my questions and see if I have anything else, but we might be at the end.
Oh.

Okay. I have maybe one final set of questions. In July 2023, former Mayor Adams released a plan to support career advancement for people with disabilities. $6 million was allocated for the issuance of an RFP called Co-Designing and Delivering Inclusive Employment Programs with and for People with Disabilities. This RFP provides funding for awardees to design and implement new training and programs to help employers make their workplaces more accessible for employees with disabilities. They have to do this work in collaboration with New Yorkers with Disabilities. The RFP was released in March 2025 by the Workforce Department Corporation in collaboration with MOPD and

SBS. Awardees were scheduled to be chosen by the end of 2025. Could you share who the vendors are and details about their proposals?
The city can’t publicly disclose the winners yet, but however, we will be announcing that soon.
Got it. So would you say that you all are a little delayed?
No, it’s just that they’re finalizing the winners and that will be released soon.
And what’s the timeline of the RFP? Is it a two-year, three-year?
Yeah, so it’s actually four years. About the first year for the co-design process, pulse three years on the implementation.
Got it. And then are vendors part of the disability community?

Yeah. So, specifically we prioritize this type of experience and relationships in the scoring of the selection process. And the selection process who demonstrates

strong access to and work with people with disabilities with a clear plan to recruit members of the community to serve as a co-design process.
Got it. And do you think RFPs are an effective tool to incentivize innovation in the disability space?

I mean, for this at least I feel like it’s very effective in the sense that– so, you are involved in– like the co-design process is bottom up and values the lived experience of those people closer to the ground compared to other models which are top down and prescriptive, and so I think that has been successful at least for this one example.
And then are there other municipalities or state governments which have issued similar RFPs?
Not that we know of.
Got it. And are there other policies or programs that other municipalities are providing or have launched that we are looking at to replicate?

Yeah, so we have country-wide MOPDs and I’m meeting them for the first time next week, and it’s exciting because we can talk about these issues and if they do something that we can steal, and we do something that they can steal, we’ll make the country better.
Amazing. That's great. Alright, well, that was my final set of questions. Thank you, Commissioner Agarwal and Sara for being here and being prepared. Super appreciate it, and I’m looking forward.
Thank you very much.
Thank you.
Thank you. We’re taking a five-minute break. We’ll be back and begin public testimony. [break]

I now open the hearing for public testimony. I remind members of the public that this a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all

times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today’s hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today’s topic of the Fiscal 2026 Preliminary Budget for DOHMH and OCME. I just want to say something. There’s over 100 people signed up today. So, in order for us to get to everyone, because we have to be out of the chambers at a certain point in time, I’m going to really ask people to please keep to the two minutes. If you have longer testimony, you can submit it to us, and then we’ll make sure it gets into the record. If you have written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms. You may also email written testimony to

testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. Okay, the first panel is Trina Preor [sic], Prior, I’m sorry. I’ve been here since 8:30 this morning, so I’m lucky I know my name. There you go. Meghan Peterson, Meghan Peterson, okie dokie. And Ryan– I’m going to not do this the right way– Manganelli [sp?]. Close enough? Okay. Alright, get settled. Okay, we ready? Trina, you want to go? Great. You got to put the mic on. Okay, great.
Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Trina Pryor. First, let me address Chairman Lynn Schulman–
[interposing] Yep.

Chairwoman Tiffany Cabán, and distinguished members of the committee. I’m Trina Pryor, Secretary Treasurer of Local 372, New York City Board of Education Employees of District Council 37, AFSCME. It is an honor of Local 372 to present this testimony on behalf of the 24,000 members we represent, including 256 SAPIS, which is an acronym for Substance Abuse Prevention Intervention Specialists. Under the leadership of

our President, John D. Francois I, Local 372, we respectfully request the City of New York to fund the SAPIS program through a dollar for dollar match with the state legislature. Since 1971, SAPIS workers have provided a range of mental health and intervention services to the largest school system in the nation. Through teaching social/emotional strategies and providing behavioral support, SAPIS workers ensure that the students in New York City Public Schools are ready to learn. In a group or individual settings, SAPIS uses evidence-based programs approved by Office of Addiction Services and Supports, also known as OASAS as positive alternatives for New York City Public School students in need. SAPIS services grades K through 12 throughout all of New York City’s 32 school districts, including special education. Okay. Let me go quickly here.
I’m just going to ask you to summarize the rest of it and then submit it. Okay.

That’s what I’m trying to do. Summarize here. Okay. Local 372’s goal is to

partner with you and your colleagues in the City Council along with the mayor in making a smart investment towards the quality of life for New York City students, their families and communities at large. It remains our shared responsibility to ensure that our children meet and exceed their potential. Without SAPIS we are robbing struggling students of their opportunity to quality, competitive education, and untimely changing the trajectory of their futures. This is why local 372 again requests that the City of New York assists our efforts in pushing for a dollar for dollar match with the state legislature in this year’s budget. Right now, our budget–
[interposing] We have to–
[inaudible] Okay.
Sorry.
It’s okay.
Yeah, no. We got the gist of it, and please make sure you submit the rest of what you have.
Yes, it was going to be emailed.
Okay, great. Alright, thank you very much. Okay, Meghan?

Hi, thank you for having me. My name is Meghan Peterson. I am a Health Department Research Scientist and I am also the President of local 3005 as part of DC 37. We represent scientific and technical workers at the Health Department and Medical Examiner’s Office. I am concerned that when we need to make budgetary cuts as we’re being asked to do now through the Chief Savings Officer, we always cut staff lines and vacancies. But if we’re going to serve the public, we need to have staff, and I would urge the city to look holistically at our contract portfolios. One example that comes up for us in the union is that we have really struggled to hire nurses and administrative public health nurses which we represent in good union jobs, but we spend a lot of money on contracts to costly temp agencies for nursing staff. So, that’s one example. I also want to bring up the water ecologists who are also

represented by our local and sort of the struggles in staffing, and I just want to make the point that we can increase the number of positions and the number of staff lines that we have, but so long as those positions are being paid the wages that they are right now, we’re going to continue to suffer from high turnover, difficulty hiring, and by extension a lack of public services. That’s is all I had. Thank you.
Thank you very much. Go ahead.

Good afternoon. Thank you, Chairs Schulman, Cabán, Hanif, and committee members, for the opportunity to testify. My name is Ryan Manganelli. I’m a Senior Manager of Policy at the 32 BJ Health Fund. Our fund provides health care benefits to more than 200,000 32 BJ members and their families through contributions from over 5,000 employers. For years we’ve seen rising hospital prices in New York City drive up the cost of health benefits and squeeze wages. I’m here today to urge the Council to prioritize health care affordability in the city’s budget by fueling funding and staffing

Office of Health Care Accountability and by working with the administration to address the ongoing impact of rising hospital prices in New York City. As the city faces a budget deficit and rising health care costs, it’s important more than ever to lean on the Office of Healthcare Accountability which is tasked with providing the Council with recommendations on the portion of health care costs spent on hospital care and convening key stakeholders to examine the cost of health care services in a city. Last year, the office published its first report on health care cost drivers affirming that the city plan also faces health care cost growth driven by high and rising hospital prices. Similar to other commercial payers from 2022 to 2024, the city employee’s PPO health plan paid New York City area hospitals more than two and a half times the price of Medicare on average. Hospital prices varied widely by system from under two times Medicare at Mount Sinai compared to three times Medicare at Montefiore Health System. We urge the Council to act by asking the largest hospital systems to explain these prices and their impact on employers and wages. The city and all New Yorkers

need relief from unaffordable hospital prices at our leading hospitals, and the relief cannot wait any longer. Thank you.
